title: Egg and Cress Sandwich
subtitle: Creamy egg mayonnaise with snipped cress on soft white bread
excerpt: The egg and cress sandwich is boiled egg mashed with mayonnaise and a little mustard, layered with snipped cress on soft white bread. The cress adds a peppery freshness that lifts the richness of the egg. It is a staple of British afternoon teas, high-street sandwich counters, and home lunch boxes.
sourceNotes: The egg mayonnaise sandwich is a British home-cooking classic; Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, documented boiled-egg preparations. The specific combination of egg mayo and mustard cress became a British standard in the twentieth century and remains one of the most popular pre-made sandwich fillings in the UK.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The egg filling keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days. Assemble the sandwich just before eating to keep the bread from going soggy.

content.text: An egg and cress sandwich is boiled eggs mashed with mayonnaise and English mustard, then layered with snipped cress on soft white bread. The cress cuts through the richness of the egg filling with a mild pepperiness. Hard-boiled eggs with a fully set yolk are the standard here: soft yolks would make the filling too liquid to spread neatly.

Place {{eggs}} eggs in a small saucepan and cover with cold water. Bring to a rolling boil over a high heat. Reduce to a steady simmer and cook for 9 minutes for a fully set yolk. Drain and cool under cold running water for 2 minutes, then peel.

Roughly chop the eggs, then mash with a fork in a small bowl until broken up but still with some texture. Add {{mayonnaise}} of mayonnaise and {{english-mustard}} of English mustard and stir through. Season with salt and a pinch of black pepper. The filling should be creamy but spreadable, not wet.

Butter all four slices of bread to the edges. Spread the egg filling generously over two slices. Scatter {{cress}} of snipped cress over the egg. Press the remaining two slices of bread on top and cut each sandwich into four fingers or two triangles.

items.symptom: The yolks are grey around the edge
items.cause: The eggs were cooked too long or cooled too slowly in the hot water.
items.fix: Drain and run cold water over the eggs immediately after the timer goes. A grey ring is harmless but means the egg was slightly overcooked. Aim for 9 minutes at a gentle simmer.

items.symptom: The filling is too wet and soaks the bread
items.cause: Too much mayonnaise, or the eggs were under-boiled and still moist inside.
items.fix: Use a fully hard-boiled egg and measure the mayonnaise. Two tablespoons for three eggs is the right ratio for a firm, spreadable filling.

items.symptom: The eggs are hard to peel
items.cause: Very fresh eggs peel poorly when hard-boiled. The membrane sticks to the white.
items.fix: Eggs a few days old peel more cleanly. Cool in cold water for at least 2 minutes before peeling, then start peeling from the wider end where there is an air pocket.

items.cause: The seasoning was skipped, or the mustard was omitted.
items.fix: Season the filling properly with salt and pepper before assembling. The mustard adds the savoury bite that makes egg mayo taste complete rather than plain.

content.text: The egg and cress sandwich is central to the British afternoon tea spread alongside cucumber and smoked salmon triangles. Cut into slim fingers rather than halves, it appears on tiered stands alongside scones and cakes. Outside the formal register it is a lunch counter staple. Mustard cress, the small peppery sprout sold in little plastic punnets, is the classic choice; watercress works if you prefer a stronger flavour. Chives or a little spring onion can replace the cress entirely for a slightly different character.
